rationale: Two sources the earlier pass could not open are now in hand as retrieved text: Nemoy's 1939 translation of al-Suyūṭī's Tuḥfat al-kirām (both al-Maʾmūn entries, pp. 24–25 and 28–29 of Isis, [p. 9] and [p. 13–14] of the PDF) and Sessa et al. 2026 (Sci. Rep. 16:12586, via the PMC open-access copy). Together with the khufupyramid.dk transcription of Petrie and the abstract page of Davidovits & Davidovits 2020, they let this pass record: (1) that the medieval compilation most often cited for the al-Maʾmūn breach describes fire, vinegar, iron tools, catapults, a well, chambers, a jar of dinars and a covered granite basin but no salt, and dates the caliph's arrival to 217/832 — supporting a date correction to GEO-C003; (2) that the proponent page carrying the salt report cites no author, work or edition; (3) that halite is confirmed as the Queen's Chamber efflorescence phase, is reported as an inherent sedimentary constituent of Giza nummulitic limestone (Klemm & Klemm as cited by Sessa), and is documented at other Egyptian limestone sites including the Sphinx — the comparator GEO-C506 previously lacked; (4) that the 1995–97 interventions inside Khufu are undocumented, a concrete instance for GEO-C594; and (5) the proponents' 2020 Pumapunku model, now entered with the correct direction toward GEO-C903. Cooperson, Legon, Túnyi & El-hemaly, Demortier, Janusek et al., Kelany et al., the Petrie scan, Klemm & Klemm, Hemeda & Sonbol and Isbell & Burkholder were not retrievable and stay blocked with routes. No edition is proposed: the additions deepen the salt line, which the assessment already treats as a weakest link, and the article's statements remain literally true; the Andean and paleomagnetic narrative changes the report wants rest entirely on unretrieved sources.

sources.title: The Treatise on the Egyptian Pyramids (Tuḥfat al-kirām fī khabar al-ahrām)
reliabilityNotes: Isis 30(1):17–37 (Feb. 1939), University of Chicago Press for the History of Science Society; JSTOR stable URL http://www.jstor.org/stable/225578. Retrieved as a 22-page archive.org PDF whose page numbers [p. N] differ from the Isis pagination (PDF [p. 9] = Isis p. 24).

A 15th-century compilation of earlier Arabic authors (al-Masʿūdī, al-Maqrīzī, Ibn Faḍl Allāh, al-Zamakhsharī and others); Nemoy notes (Isis p. 18) that al-Suyūṭī does not always name his authorities. It is not itself a contemporary witness to the 9th-century breach.
OCR of the scan is imperfect (e.g. 'AL-MA'MiYN' for al-Maʾmūn); quotations here are copied from the retrieved text as shown.

sources.title: Material characterization of stone surfaces in the inner chambers of the Khufu (Cheops) Pyramid: towards informed conservation strategies
reliabilityNotes: Scientific Reports 16:12586 (16 April 2026), CC BY 4.0; text read via the open-access PMC copy (PMC13087131) located through OpenAlex. Locators below name article sections, not pages.

Conservation-science paper by the ScanPyramids mission (TUM / Cairo University); it does not address the casting hypothesis and takes the natural origin of the limestone as given. Its statements about halite in Giza bedrock are second-hand citations of Klemm & Klemm 2010 and Hemeda & Sonbol 2020, neither read here.

Sampling was limited to efflorescence and naturally detached, salt-affected fragments (no stone cores); XRD detection limit stated as below 5 wt%; portable XRF in ambient air cannot see Na or Mg. Data available only on request and with Egyptian ministry permission.

sources.title: The Queen´s Chamber — Pyramid of Khufu (Cheops): dimensions, with transcribed passages from Petrie 1883 §§41–44
reliabilityNotes: Amateur metrological website; the value here is its transcription of W. M. F. Petrie, The Pyramids and Temples of Gizeh (1883), §41 (p. 66), §42 (pp. 67–69) and §43 (pp. 69–70), each passage tagged with a locator code of the form (S5orig-[S41]-P66-L29-37).

The original 1883 scan was not shown; the transcription has not been checked against it. The site author's own remarks (e.g. that most of the walls are covered with salt incrustation) are his observations, not Petrie's, and are labelled as such below.
The site's cubit-conversion commentary and drawings are the author's interpretation and are not used here.

evidence.title: Al-Suyūṭī's two al-Maʾmūn entries (tr. Nemoy 1939) describe the breach and its finds but mention no salt
evidence.sourceStatement: The compilation gives the caliph's opening of the pyramid twice. In the first entry (Isis p. 24, attributed by Nemoy's n.6 to al-Masʿūdī via al-Maqrīzī) the workers kindled fire, applied vinegar, tempered iron tools and used catapults; the Pyramid was opened "and they found its wall to be twenty cubits thick"; behind the breach they found a chrysolite jar of a thousand dinars, a square well with four doors to chambers of shrouded corpses, and at the top a chamber with a stone sarcophagus holding a malachite idol. In the second entry (Isis pp. 28–29, [p. 13–14]) al-Maʾmūn struck a narrow shaft of black quartz, a deep well, and a square place with a covered granite basin: "they found nothing but worn out pieces of rope". A third mention (Ibn al-Mutawwaj, Isis p. 30) reports a sarcophagus with an inscribed marble tablet. No passage in any of these mentions salt, halite, or any coating on the chamber walls.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: the salt-layer report attributed to al-Maʾmūn's party (GEO-C003, carried in the ledger only by SRC-GEOPOLYMER-INST) is absent from the compilation that gathers the principal medieval Arabic accounts of the breach. This is negative evidence within one compilation, not proof that no Arabic author says it: al-Maqrīzī's full Khiṭaṭ chapter (Graefe ed.), ʿAbd al-Laṭīf al-Baghdādī and the Arabic extracts in Vyse 1840 vol. 2 remain unread (GEO-R001). But the burden now sits with whoever asserts the salt report to name its author.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 9] (Isis p. 24, first al-Maʾmūn entry, quote 'they found its wall to be twenty cubits thick'); second entry at [p. 13–14] (Isis pp. 28–29)
limitations: A 15th-century compilation of earlier authors, translated in 1939; not a contemporary witness.
Other medieval Arabic sources on the breach have not been checked in this pass.
OCR of the scan is imperfect; readings of names are Nemoy's transliterations as rendered by OCR.

evidence.title: Nemoy dates al-Maʾmūn's arrival in Egypt to 217/832, not 820
evidence.sourceStatement: Nemoy's footnote 7 to the first al-Maʾmūn entry identifies the caliph as son of Hārūn al-Rashīd, 170/786–218/833, and states that he "came down to Egypt to suppress a rebellion early in 217/832". The text itself gives no year for the opening of the pyramid.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: the '820 AD' in GEO-C003 comes from the proponent web page (SRC-GEOPOLYMER-INST) and matches no source in this record; the translator's dating of the caliph's Egyptian stay to AH 217 (AD 832) is the only dated statement shown. This bears on the claim's date, not on the salt. A correction of the claim's date is proposed on this basis.
limitations: The date is the translator's note, not the medieval text; the report also names Cooperson as dating the visit to early 832, but that chapter was not retrievable.
The footnote dates the caliph's entry into Egypt, not explicitly the day the pyramid was breached.

evidence.title: The proponent page carrying the al-Maʾmūn salt report cites no medieval source, dates it to 820, and dismisses the sedimentary reading without argument
evidence.sourceStatement: The page states that Caliph Al Mamun, "when he opened in 820 AD the Great Pyramid", found in the interior rooms that the stone was "covered with a layer of 1.5 cm thick cooking salt", halite NaCl. No author, work, manuscript or edition is given for this description. In the same passage the page rejects the Egyptologists' view that NaCl is expected because the limestones were deposited in salty seas as 'silly reasoning', arguing that if so "all our cathedrals built with limestone should be covered with salt", and dismisses the visitor-urine explanation as equally silly.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: the ledger's only carrier of the salt-layer report is an uncited statement on a proponent web page; combined with GEO-E601 (absence from al-Suyūṭī's compilation) this leaves GEO-C003 with no traceable medieval anchor. The page's comparator argument (European cathedrals) is the wrong control for Giza limestone; SRC-SESSA-2026 (GEO-E605, GEO-E606) supplies the Egyptian comparators and the sedimentary-halite reading the page dismisses.
evidence.exactLocator: Section 'Why is it meaningful?' and following paragraph beginning 'The presence of NaCl salt is just an anecdote for Egyptology'
limitations: Proponent web page (Geopolymer Institute, dated 10 Apr 2006), not a scholarly publication.
The absence of a citation on the page does not itself establish that no medieval source exists.

evidence.title: Efflorescence on Queen's Chamber limestone is halite (XRD: halite, calcite, quartz only)
evidence.sourceStatement: The authors state that in the Queen's Chamber "halite was identified as the main phase responsible for efflorescence" on the limestone blocks. Targeted SEM-EDX of white efflorescence (samples S4, S5) detected only Na and Cl, with a Na–Cl correlation of R = 0.969 across all samples and halite whiskers visible at 400× and 1600× (Fig. 5); XRD of seven samples "confirmed the presence of only halite, calcite, and quartz", with no nitrates and no evidence of widespread gypsum formation.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: this confirms the presence component of GEO-C506 — the salt on Great Pyramid chamber stone is NaCl — with modern instrumentation rather than a taste test. It carries essentially no weight toward casting: the same paper reads the halite as native to the limestone (GEO-E606) and the study analysed surface efflorescence and detached fragments only, so it cannot say whether NaCl is bulk-distributed or surface-confined.
evidence.exactLocator: Abstract; 'Samples investigation: SEM-EDX and XRD analysis'; Figs. 5–7 — via open-access copy PMC13087131
limitations: Only efflorescence and naturally detached, salt-affected fragments were analysed; no stone was cored, so bulk versus surface distribution is untested.
XRD detection limit below 5 wt%; minor sulfate phases could be missed (the authors say so).
Conservation study; not designed to test any origin hypothesis for the blocks.

evidence.title: Halite efflorescence is documented at other Egyptian limestone sites, including the carved-bedrock Sphinx
evidence.sourceStatement: The authors write that "Halite has been frequently identified as a dominant salt" contributing to efflorescence at numerous heritage sites across Egypt, and list its documentation at the Menkaure Pyramid, the Sphinx in Giza, the White Monastery in Sohag, the Imni Tomb at Lisht and the Saqqara Pyramid, citing published studies for each.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: GEO-C506 asserts that comparable natural limestone monuments do not exhibit the Great Pyramid's surface NaCl; the proponents' comparator was European cathedrals. Egyptian limestone sites in the same climate — including the Sphinx, carved from Giza bedrock and claimed by no one to be cast, and rock-cut tombs — show the same halite efflorescence. This is a literature summary in a conservation paper, not a controlled comparison of concentrations, so it undermines the comparator premise without measuring it.
evidence.exactLocator: Section 'Queen's Chamber and thieves' corridor', paragraph beginning 'Halite has been frequently identified' — via open-access copy PMC13087131
limitations: Second-hand: the authors cite other studies (refs 15, 19, 42–44) which were not read here.
No concentrations are compared; the statement is qualitative.
Menkaure is itself among the pyramids proponents claim, so that comparator does not discriminate; the Sphinx and the tombs do.

evidence.title: Halite reported as a primary sedimentary constituent of Giza nummulitic limestone (Klemm & Klemm, as cited by Sessa et al.)
evidence.sourceStatement: SEM-EDX of naturally detached material from visually unaffected areas of the substrate (S1–S3) found Na and Cl among the elements present, which the authors say indicates these "are probably inherent components of the stone matrix". They report Hemeda & Sonbol's composition of Khufu backing blocks (calcite with minor iron oxides, quartz, dolomite, opaques and halite) and state that Klemm & Klemm describe halite as the primary salt in the nummulitic limestones of the Giza plateau, its presence within the stratigraphic layers suggesting it is part of the original sedimentary environment, "likely precipitated from evaporating marine or lagoonal waters" during rock formation.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: if halite is native to the strata conventionally identified as the pyramid's source rock, then salt on the blocks is expected under the carved account and GEO-C506's comparative premise fails; the proponent page's dismissal of exactly this reading (GEO-E603) is met here by a stated geological mechanism. The decisive check remains GEO-R010 — halite in unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock and quarry faces — and Klemm & Klemm 2010 should be read directly. Note that both the proponents and this reading predict NaCl in the blocks; the salt does not discriminate between them.
evidence.exactLocator: Section 'Samples investigation: SEM-EDX and XRD analysis', first paragraph — via open-access copy PMC13087131
limitations: Klemm & Klemm 2010 and Hemeda & Sonbol 2020 are cited, not read; the halite-in-strata statement is second-hand.
'Inherent components' is the authors' inference from detached fragments, not from cored stone.
Standardless SEM-EDX quantification with ZAF corrections; semi-quantitative.

evidence.title: A stated natural origin for pyramid halite narrows the salt-based support for cast limestone
evidence.sourceStatement: As above: the authors treat the Queen's Chamber halite as a soluble salt inherent to the limestone matrix, mobilised by humidity (deliquescence relative humidity of NaCl ≈ 75%) and visitor-driven condensation, and cite Klemm & Klemm for halite as a primary constituent of Giza nummulitic limestone "likely precipitated from evaporating marine or lagoonal waters". The paper does not mention any artificial-stone hypothesis.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: GEO-C020 is supported in the ledger partly through the salt line (GEO-E004, GEO-E026, via GEO-C003/GEO-C506). A geological origin for the halite, stated by non-proponent geologists, removes the premise that salt on the blocks is anomalous for quarried limestone. It does not test any block for a binder and so cannot by itself undermine GEO-C020; it limits what the salt can show.
evidence.exactLocator: Sections 'Samples investigation: SEM-EDX and XRD analysis' and 'Queen's Chamber and thieves' corridor' (DRH discussion) — via open-access copy PMC13087131
limitations: Indirect: bears on one evidential line for GEO-C020, not on the blocks' microstructure or binder chemistry.
Second-hand citation of Klemm & Klemm 2010.

evidence.title: Undocumented 1995–97 interventions and recurrent efflorescence inside the Khufu pyramid
evidence.sourceStatement: The authors state that documentation of the "conservation interventions carried out between 1995 and 1997 is not available", but that published photographs and later documentation make it evident that "surface cleaning and the filling of wall cavities were carried out". XRF points P27–P28 show a sulfur enrichment at a visibly restored area, which they read as an S-rich (likely gypsum-bearing) fill not part of the original stone. In 2022 salt formation was observed only in very limited areas; since then "extensive salt efflorescence is now visible on the stone surfaces" (Fig. 3, Supplementary Fig. S4). Graffiti residues predating 2004 also survive.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: a concrete instance of GEO-C594 at the most-cited monument in the case — the interior was cleaned and patched in the 1990s with no available record, and the salt now visible re-formed within about two years. Any surface-salt observation at Giza (including Davidovits' 1984–2003 taste tests, GEO-E026) is therefore a post-cleaning or between-cleaning observation whose baseline is unknown, and a sulfur-rich modern fill is present on the very walls.
evidence.exactLocator: Section 'Queen's Chamber and thieves' corridor', first paragraph, and 'In-situ XRF analysis' (P27–P28) — via open-access copy PMC13087131
limitations: The authors infer the nature of the 1990s work from photographs; the intervention records themselves were not seen by them or by us.
Concerns one monument's interior; GEO-C594 is a general claim about megalithic sites.

evidence.title: Petrie (1883) recorded salt incrustation in the Queen's Chamber and on the two lower laps of its niche (via transcription)
evidence.sourceStatement: The page transcribes Petrie §41 (p. 66) giving the Queen's Chamber size "after allowing suitably in each part for the incrustation of salt", and §43 (pp. 69–70) stating that the niche dimensions are corrected for the salt exudation on the two lower laps and that "there is no salt on the upper three laps". The site author separately remarks that the greater part of the walls is covered with salt incrustation, making joints hard to find.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: salt on the Queen's Chamber walls was thick enough in 1880–82 to require metrological correction, so the phenomenon predates mass tourism and the 1990s cleaning — this supports the presence component of GEO-C506 and retires the visitor-urine explanation as sufficient. Petrie's note that the upper three laps of the niche carried no salt is a height-dependent distribution consistent with the humidity-driven efflorescence gradient Sessa et al. describe (GEO-E604) and is not predicted by salt bound uniformly in cast stone. Zero diagnosticity for casting either way.
evidence.exactLocator: Sections 5.8.4 and 5.8.14, transcribed passages tagged (S5orig-[S41]-P66-L29-37) and (S5orig-[S43]-P69-L31-40 and P70-L1-11)
limitations: Transcription on an amateur website; the 1883 scan was not shown and the wording is unverified against it.
Petrie records salt at 1880–82, a millennium after the al-Maʾmūn breach; it does not speak to GEO-C003's medieval accounts.

evidence.title: Proponents' 2020 Pumapunku model: natural Khapia andesite sand stored at Iwawe (Stratum V), piedras cansadas not used
evidence.sourceStatement: The abstract states that to make geopolymer andesite around AD 600–700 the builders could have transported an andesite stony material with the consistency of sand from the Cerro Khapia volcano, adding an organo-mineral binder from local biomass; that "They did not use the many quadrangular volcanic blocks", the famous piedras cansadas lying on both sides of Lake Titicaca; that they exploited a natural volcanic andesite sand from Cerro Khapia, "transported and stored it at the shore village of Iwawe", Stratum (V) in the excavation by Isbell & Burkholder (2002); and that they did not need to crush andesite rock, the sand resembling the Roman pozzolana called carbunculus.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: this is the primary statement of the model GEO-C903 describes, so it supports that descriptive claim directly. It also fixes two checkable objects: the Iwawe Stratum V deposit (GEO-R009) and the abandoned quadrangular blocks. Both parties now place the andesite's origin at Khapia/Ccapia, which is why quarry geochemistry alone cannot separate them (GEO-C030 in its narrow form).
evidence.exactLocator: Abstract on the geopolymer.org library page for GPSA 2020, Vol. 1, pp. 36–43
limitations: Abstract only; the PDF (DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.10021.93929/2) returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
Proponent-authored, self-published journal (Journal on Geopolymer Science Applied to Archaeology).

evidence.title: Proponents restate that Parts I–III showed Pumapunku stones to be artificial geopolymers
evidence.sourceStatement: The abstract opens: the studies carried out in 2017–2018 on the monumental stones of Pumapunku "provided evidence that the stones are ancient artificial geopolymers" (Parts I to III).
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: a restatement by the same team of the results already entered as GEO-E006 and GEO-E007; it adds no new observation and carries no independent weight toward GEO-C021. Recorded so that the model's continuity with the earlier papers is on the ledger, and because the default is in.
evidence.exactLocator: Abstract, first sentence, geopolymer.org library page
limitations: Self-citation of the authors' own prior work; not new evidence.
Abstract only.

research.title: Survey Cerro Khapia (Ccapia) for andesite extraction faces versus natural sand deposits
research.summary: Both the orthodox provenance work and the proponents' 2020 model place the Pumapunku/Tiwanaku andesite's origin on Cerro Khapia; they differ on what was taken from it — dressed blocks from quarry faces, or a natural volcanic sand needing no crushing (GEO-E610). A field survey of the mountain's andesite outcrops for extraction signatures (working faces, wedge or pounder scars, dressing debris, abandoned blocks matched in size to monument ashlars) versus loose scoria/sand deposits, with grain-size and petrographic comparison of any sand against the Iwawe Stratum V material (GEO-R009), would settle which material left the mountain. Pairs with a literature check of any post-2013 fieldwork documenting Khapia quarries.
research.informationGain: Documented quarry faces with dressing debris and en-route ashlars would show carved andesite leaving Khapia and remove the proponents' aggregate-source story; a mountain with no extraction surfaces but a natural sand matching Iwawe Stratum V would remove the orthodox account's quarry and leave the proponents' model live. Either result is legible without touching a monument stone.
